title: Quentin and the Language
premise: Rafael Dunmore, a celebrated restaurant critic who lost the ability to taste after a childhood rupture they have never named, has built a life on precise, borrowed language — describing flavors they cannot feel. When the house where they grew up goes to auction, Rafael is summoned back as executor of an estate that includes not just property but an unresolved wrong: decades ago, their testimony — or silence — destroyed another family. As the sale deadline approaches, Rafael must find the surviving member of that family, learn what actually happened the night the story went wrong, and decide whether truth can be spoken without becoming another kind of violence. The novel ends with Rafael standing in the emptied house, speaking aloud for the first time what they witnessed, and tasting — faintly, unmistakably — salt.
about_author: Mirabel Whitlock is the pen name of a former court stenographer who spent eleven years transcribing other people's confessions before writing her own fiction. She lives in a coastal town whose name she declines to publish, and this is her second novel.

chapters.title: The Inventory of Unsaid Things
chapters.summary: Rafael's POV. We meet them mid-review, describing a tasting menu in gorgeous language while privately unable to taste anything. At home, they maintain literal notebooks of sentences never spoken. Emotional beat: elegant numbness, the reader senses a wound beneath the polish.

chapters.title: Notice of Sale
chapters.summary: Rafael's POV. A certified letter arrives: the childhood house at 14 Alder Lane enters probate auction, and Rafael, named in the will of the late owner Mrs. Halloway, must attend. They burn dinner without noticing. Beat: dread disguised as administrative annoyance.

chapters.title: Auction Terms
chapters.summary: Rafael's POV, with a flashback thread. Rafael researches the property and finds their own name in an old newspaper clipping about 'the incident' — redacted even in memory. Their editor calls; Rafael cancels three reviews. Beat: the past asserting jurisdiction.

chapters.title: The House Remembers Differently
chapters.summary: Rafael returns to the town; the house smells of cedar and something they can almost taste. Neighbors recognize them with warmth that feels like accusation. Beat: uncanny belonging — home as both refuge and crime scene.

chapters.title: What the Neighbor Saw
chapters.summary: Alternating POV: Dolores Vann, now elderly, remembers the night Rafael's family left town. She offers kindness laced with questions. Rafael deflects with charm. Beat: first collision between Rafael's curated story and someone else's memory.

chapters.title: The Other Family
chapters.summary: Rafael's POV. Records reveal the Okonkwo family lost the house after an accusation — one Rafael's parents made, and child-Rafael corroborated. The son, Emeka, was Rafael's best friend. Beat: guilt arriving with a face attached.

chapters.title: Finding Emeka
chapters.summary: Emeka's POV. He runs a small bakery two towns over; he tastes everything deliberately, a quiet defiance. He recognizes Rafael instantly and serves them bread without a word. Beat: charged silence, hospitality as challenge.

chapters.title: Bread and Testimony
chapters.summary: Two POVs interleaved. Emeka finally speaks: he doesn't want apology, he wants the record corrected — his mother died believing herself disgraced. Rafael admits they don't remember testifying. Beat: the horror of a hole where memory should be.

chapters.title: What Children Are Asked
chapters.summary: Rafael's POV, deep flashback. Eleven-year-old Rafael, coached by parents, repeating words given to them by adults after the fire in the Halloways' garage. The taste vanished that week. Beat: the wound located — complicity without understanding.

chapters.title: The Auction Opens
chapters.summary: Ensemble scene at the courthouse steps. Bidders circle 14 Alder Lane; a developer leads. Rafael holds proxy power to delay the sale but using it exposes the old case publicly. Beat: ticking clock made legal and literal.

chapters.title: Dolores's Version
chapters.summary: Dolores POV. She tells Rafael what the town said versus what she saw: Rafael's father moving boxes from the garage the night before the fire. She stayed silent too, out of fear. Beat: shared complicity, unexpected alliance forming.

chapters.title: The Review I Cannot Write
chapters.summary: Rafael's POV. Back in the city, Rafael submits a review so hollow their editor calls it 'the worst thing you've written.' They realize the language they hid inside has stopped working entirely. Beat: collapse of the false self.

chapters.title: Emeka's Condition
chapters.summary: Emeka POV. He agrees to help reopen the record only if Rafael testifies to what they were told to say — naming their own parents. Rafael resists: it feels like betrayal. Beat: justice demanding a price from the person seeking it.

chapters.title: Mother's Telephone Voice
chapters.summary: Rafael calls their mother, ostensibly about estate paperwork. She is warm, deflecting, revisionist. Rafael asks one direct question and receives a monologue about loyalty. Beat: the machinery of silence shown still running.

chapters.title: The Garage Floor
chapters.summary: Rafael breaks into the sealed house at night. In the old garage, under paint layers, they find scorch marks and a child's chalk drawing preserved behind a board — drawn by Emeka, addressed to Rafael. Beat: grief breaking through numbness; a phantom taste of chalk dust.

chapters.title: Delay Granted
chapters.summary: Rafael files to delay the auction citing disputed estate contents, forcing a public records review — which reopens the arson file. The developer's lawyer threatens suit. Beat: point of no return; Rafael chooses exposure over safety.

chapters.title: Father Comes to Town
chapters.summary: Two-hander confrontation. Rafael's father arrives to 'manage' them, offering money for the house and a rehearsed version of history. Rafael, for once, says nothing — letting the silence do its work. Beat: inversion; silence becomes Rafael's weapon instead of cage.

chapters.title: Deposition
chapters.summary: Climax begins. Under formal questioning, Rafael recounts the coaching, the fire, the false statement — voice failing, then steadying. Emeka watches from the gallery. Beat: the unsaid inventory read aloud, item by item.

chapters.title: What the Fire Was For
chapters.summary: Climax resolves. Evidence confirms the father's insurance fraud; the Okonkwo name is formally cleared. It is not triumphant — the mother stops calling, the town splits. Emeka tells Rafael it was enough. Beat: justice outside the law completed by the law, but paid for personally.

chapters.title: The Last Bid
chapters.summary: The auction resumes. Rafael, authorized by the cleared estate terms, sells the house to Emeka below market, funding it partly with their own savings. The developer walks away furious. Beat: restitution as act, not speech; belonging offered rather than claimed.

chapters.title: Salt
chapters.summary: Rafael's POV. In the emptied house, Rafael speaks aloud the full confession to no one — every entry in the inventory — then eats bread Emeka baked, standing in the bare kitchen. They taste it: salt, crust, wheat. Beat: catharsis; the tongue returning as the truth leaves.

chapters.title: A New Vocabulary
chapters.summary: Epilogue, Rafael's POV. Months later, Rafael publishes a final column announcing retirement from criticism — 'I am done describing things I cannot feel' — and takes a small job teaching writing to teenagers in Emeka's town. Beat: quiet resolution; identity rebuilt on presence rather than performance.
